overview:
Moses tells Israel the covenant made at Horeb was made with the people standing before him, not just with their parents. He repeats the Ten Commandments the LORD spoke out of the fire and recalls that God wrote them on two tablets and “added no more.” The leaders, afraid the fire would consume them, begged Moses to go near, listen for them, and report back, and they promised to obey. God approved, wished they would always have such a heart, and kept Moses with him to receive the rest of the law.

The commandments are not repeated word for word. The Sabbath is to be kept as well as remembered (v. 12), and its reason is Israel's slavery in Egypt, where Exodus gives God's rest at creation (v. 15; Exodus 20:11). The day of rest is turned toward those who most need it: “that thy manservant and thy maidservant may rest as well as thou” (v. 14).

historicalContext.label: Author
historicalContext.text: Presented as Moses' speeches; the book says Moses wrote “this law” (31:9) and narrates his death. Jewish and Christian tradition credits Moses; many scholars connect its core with the law book found under Josiah (2 Kings 22).

historicalContext.label: Date written
historicalContext.text: Unknown. Tradition places it in Moses' lifetime (15th or 13th century BC); many scholars date its core to the 7th century BC, with additions in the 6th.

historicalContext.label: Date of events
historicalContext.text: Spoken in the fortieth year (1:3), recalling Horeb nearly forty years earlier (Exodus 19:1). Reckoning from 1 Kings 6:1 gives about 1406 BC for the speech; many scholars prefer the 13th century BC.

historicalContext.label: Setting (events)
historicalContext.text: The valley opposite Beth-peor (4:46). The scene recalled is the foot of the burning mountain, with Moses standing between God and the people (vv. 4–5, 23).

historicalContext.label: Parallel accounts
historicalContext.text: Exodus 20:1–21. Abinadi's recital in Mosiah 12:34–36 and 13:12–24 follows the Exodus wording.

hermeneutics:
Ancient treaties bound more than the people who swore them. Esarhaddon's succession treaties of 672 BC made vassals swear for their sons and grandsons not yet born, and Hittite kings reissued a treaty when a vassal's son took the throne, restating the father's terms in the son's name. Verse 3 does both at once: the covenant at Horeb is “with us, even us,” the living, though most who stood at Horeb have died (2:14–16). Each generation stands at the mountain again.

Babylonian texts know a day called *shapattu*, the fifteenth of the month, when the moon was full, described as a day for quieting the god's heart. It was a lunar feast, not a weekly rest for workers. Israel's Sabbath counts sevens without regard to the moon, and Deuteronomy gives it a social reason: servants, foreigners, and working animals rest because Israel itself was a slave in Egypt (vv. 14–15). Where law collections like Hammurabi's treated slaves as property, this command gives them a day of their own.

Letters from Mari in the 18th century BC show how a god's word usually reached people: a prophet received it, and an official wrote it down and sent it on to the king. Horeb begins the other way round. The whole assembly hears God directly (vv. 4, 22), and only afterward, at the people's request, does Moses become the go-between (vv. 23–27), with God's approval (v. 28). Deuteronomy grounds Moses' role as mediator in this request, as 18:16–18 recalls.

structure.summary: An inclusio: God speaking “out of the midst of the fire” frames the commandments (vv. 4–5, 22–27).

notes: **The Sabbath at the center:** the Sabbath's “manservant,” “maidservant,” “ox,” and “ass” (v. 14) reappear in the last command (v. 21). Norbert Lohfink argued that this makes the Sabbath the hinge of Deuteronomy's version.
**Thy God:** “the LORD thy God” occurs 9 times in vv. 6–16, against 5 in Exodus 20:2–12. The four extra uses all fall in vv. 12–16.
**Joined commands:** vv. 18–21 each open with “Neither” (Hebrew “and not”), chaining the last commands together; Exodus 20:14–17 lists them separately.

The unit begins with the new heading at 4:44 and ends at 5:33, once Moses has explained why he, not God, now speaks the statutes. At 6:1 “Now these are the commandments” opens the teaching that follows.
**Backward:** Exodus 20:1–21. **Forward:** Deuteronomy 18:15–18 recalls the people's request at Horeb (vv. 23–27) as the reason God will raise up a prophet like Moses.

traditions.text: When Abinadi reads the commandments to King Noah's priests, his wording follows Exodus, not this chapter. He says “Remember the sabbath day,” grounds it in the six days of creation, and puts the neighbor's house before his wife. The Book of Mormon's one full recital of the commandments thus preserves the Exodus 20 form, though Abinadi is speaking to Nephites who also had the five books of Moses on the brass plates (1 Nephi 5:11).

This revelation says that without the higher priesthood no one can see the face of God and live, and that Moses plainly taught this to Israel and sought to sanctify them so that they might behold his face. Deuteronomy's people say they have seen that God talks with man and he lives (v. 24), yet they ask Moses to go near in their place (v. 27). The revelation reads that retreat as the people's failure to endure God's presence.

How can Exodus say “Remember” and Deuteronomy “Keep” (v. 12)? A teaching quoted in the Talmud answers that God spoke both words in a single utterance, which no human mouth could say and no human ear could hear. Rav Adda bar Ahava drew a rule from the pairing: since women must keep the Sabbath, they are also bound to remember it with the blessing over the day.

Only Deuteronomy adds “as the LORD thy God hath commanded thee” to the Sabbath (v. 12). Commanded when? The Talmud, followed by Rashi, says at Marah, where God made a statute for Israel before they reached Sinai (Exodus 15:25). On v. 15 Rashi adds that God freed Israel on condition that they serve him and keep his commandments.

The rabbis compared the animals in both lists. Exodus says “thy cattle”; Deuteronomy says “thine ox, nor thine ass, nor any of thy cattle” (v. 14), and the Talmud draws rulings from each word, linking the ox to the law of muzzling and the ass to the law of unloading a burden. It also reads the closing clause, that servants may rest as well as their master, as limiting the comparison: people and animals are treated alike only in resting on the Sabbath.

Rabbi Hanina ben Agil asked why the word “good” appears with the parents command here (“that it may go well with thee,” v. 16) but not in Exodus. The answer he finally received: the first tablets were destined to be broken. Rav Ashi explained that if “good” had been written on them, good would have ended for Israel when they shattered.

A Qumran manuscript of Deuteronomy, probably a study or liturgical text, gives the Sabbath command both reasons. After the Egypt reason of v. 15 it adds the Exodus reason, that the LORD made heaven and earth in six days. Its scribe joined the two versions instead of choosing between them, much as the rabbis held “Remember” and “Keep” together (above). The manuscript is one of the clearest signs that early readers noticed the differences between the two Decalogues.

God says the people “have well said” (v. 28), but Rashi hears disappointment in Moses' telling. When they ask him to go near and speak to them (v. 27), the Hebrew uses an unusual pronoun, and Rashi says it shows they had weakened Moses, who grieved that they did not want to learn from God's own mouth out of love. Would it not have been better, Moses asks, to hear from God than from me?

Paul calls the command to honor father and mother the first commandment with promise, and gives the promise as “That it may be well with thee, and thou mayest live long.” The first half is Deuteronomy's addition (v. 16), also found in the Greek Septuagint of Exodus 20:12. His wording links the rabbis' question about “good” (above) to the version Christians read.

Hebrews recalls the mountain that burned with fire, the darkness, and the voice which those who heard begged not to hear any more. The detail matches v. 25, where the people fear that hearing the voice “any more” will kill them, and the retelling in 18:16. Hebrews sets that fear against Christians' approach to Mount Zion and to Jesus the mediator of a new covenant, a mediator greater than the one the people asked for in v. 27.
